title: How the internet was built
blurb: From a two-letter message in 1969 to the phone in your hand.

cards.text: On 29 October 1969 a computer at UCLA sent the first message over ARPANET to one at the Stanford Research Institute. The network was funded by the US defence research agency, ARPA.
The message was meant to be “LOGIN”. The system crashed after two letters, so the first word sent was “LO”.
Instead of one fixed line, messages are chopped into small packets that travel separately and are put back together at the end. If one route fails, packets take another.
British computer scientist Donald Davies, at the National Physical Laboratory, came up with the same idea independently and gave packets their name.
In 1971 Ray Tomlinson sent the first email between computers on ARPANET, and picked the @ sign to separate the person from the machine.

cards.q: What was the first word sent over ARPANET?
cards.explain: “LO”: the system crashed before “LOGIN” was finished.

points: ARPANET sent its first message in 1969
Data travels in small packets that can take any route
Email and the @ sign arrived in 1971

cards.text: By the 1970s there were many separate networks. Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn designed TCP/IP, shared rules that let any network talk to any other.
ARPANET switched to TCP/IP on 1 January 1983. Many count this as the start of the internet: a network of networks.
Every device on the internet has an IP address. The Domain Name System, from 1983, turns names such as bbc.co.uk into those numbers.
Cerf and Kahn shared the 2004 Turing Award, computing’s top prize, and received the US Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2005.

opts: Different networks talking to each other
cards.explain: It gave every network the same rules, so they could connect into one internet.

points: TCP/IP is the internet’s shared language
DNS turns names into numeric addresses

episodes.title: The web is not the internet

cards.text: In March 1989 Tim Berners-Lee, a British scientist at CERN in Switzerland, proposed a way to link documents across computers. It became the World Wide Web.
He created HTML to write pages, URLs to find them and HTTP to fetch them, along with the first web browser and web server.
The first website went public at CERN in 1991. It explained what the web was and how to use it.
In April 1993 CERN put the web’s software in the public domain, so anyone could use and build on it without paying.
The internet is the network of connected computers. The web is one service that runs on it, alongside things like email.

cards.q: Where did Tim Berners-Lee invent the web?
cards.explain: At CERN, the physics laboratory near Geneva.

points: The web was proposed in 1989 at CERN
HTML, URLs and HTTP are its building blocks
The internet is the network; the web runs on it

cards.text: Mosaic, released in 1993, showed pictures and text together and made the web easy to use. Its co-creator Marc Andreessen went on to co-found Netscape.
As the web grew, finding things got hard. Google’s founders ranked pages by how many other pages linked to them, an idea called PageRank.
Apple’s first iPhone, released in 2007, put a full web browser in a phone.
Around 2016, more web browsing worldwide began happening on phones and tablets than on computers.
Small packets, shared rules and open standards from decades ago still carry everything from video calls to this card.

cards.q: What did PageRank use to rank pages?
opts: How many other pages linked to them
cards.explain: Links from other pages, treated like votes.

points: Mosaic made the web visual in 1993
Phones overtook computers for browsing around 2016
